payload.name: voice-tremor
payload.scope: Voice tremor is a human-made clinical measure of the amplitude modulation of phonation — the cycle-to-cycle variation in the fundamental frequency and intensity of the voice signal — devised to quantify shaky voice in voice-disorder assessment.

definition.body: Voice tremor is a human-made measure of the amplitude modulation of phonation: the cycle-to-cycle variation in the fundamental frequency and intensity of the voice signal produced by the vocal folds. It is computed from a recorded voice signal by tracking the fundamental frequency across successive glottal cycles and measuring the amplitude of each cycle; the tremor rate is the number of modulation cycles per second and the tremor amplitude is the peak-to-peak variation expressed as a percentage of the mean amplitude. It persists as a standardized parameter in clinical voice assessment because it is defined by a repeatable measurement procedure applied to a recorded voice sample. e.g.: voice tremor measured in a patient with spasmodic dysphonia during a clinical voice assessment; tremor amplitude reported as a percentage in a voice disorder diagnostic report; a voice tremor standard used by a speech-language pathologist to quantify shaky voice | not: jitter (frequency modulation of the fundamental frequency); shimmer (intensity modulation of the voice signal) [formal: tremor | substrate: behavior | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

definition.body: Voice range profile is a human-made graph that maps a speaker's voice across pitch and loudness: the range of fundamental frequencies a voice can produce at each loudness level, plotted as a region in the frequency-intensity plane. It is generated by recording a voice while the speaker phonates sustained vowels across a pitch and loudness sweep, measuring the fundamental frequency and sound pressure level at each point, and plotting the outermost boundary of the achievable region. definition.body: Voice break is a human-made clinical event in phonation: the abrupt, involuntary interruption or discontinuity in the voice signal during sustained phonation or pitch gliding, caused by laryngeal muscle fatigue or dysfunction. It is observed as a sudden drop in intensity, a sudden shift to falsetto, or a complete cessation of phonation at a particular pitch or loudness level. It persists as a recognized clinical sign because it is defined by an observable auditory and acoustic event during voice assessment. e.g.: a voice break heard during a sustained vowel phonation in a patient with vocal fold paresis; a voice break observed during a pitch glide in a voice disorder assessment; a voice break documented in a clinical voice evaluation report | not: jitter (cycle-to-cycle frequency variation, not an interruption of phonation); phonation arrest (complete cessation of phonation due to vocal fold adduction failure, not a momentary break) [formal: vocis interruptus | substrate: behavior | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

definition.body: Formant frequency is a human-made acoustic parameter of speech: a resonance frequency of the vocal tract that appears as a concentration of energy in the speech spectrum. It is measured from a recorded speech signal by identifying the peaks in the spectral envelope — the local maxima of the magnitude spectrum — and is labeled F1, F2, F3, etc. in order of increasing frequency. It persists as a standardized speech parameter because it is defined by a repeatable spectral analysis procedure applied to a recorded utterance. e.g.: the first formant frequency measured in a vowel produced by a speaker during a speech analysis; the formant frequency values used in a speech recognition system to distinguish vowel sounds; a formant frequency measured in a clinical voice assessment to evaluate vocal tract configuration | not: fundamental frequency (the vibration rate of the vocal folds, not a vocal tract resonance); harmonic (an integer multiple of the fundamental frequency, not a vocal tract resonance peak) [formal: formanta | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: speaking-fundamental-frequency
payload.scope: Speaking fundamental frequency is a human-made acoustic parameter — the average fundamental frequency of the voice signal during connected speech — devised to characterize a speaker's voice in speech analysis.

definition.body: Speaking fundamental frequency is a human-made acoustic parameter of speech: the average fundamental frequency of the voice signal during connected speech, measured as the mean of the fundamental frequency values across a sample of continuous speech. It is computed from a recorded speech sample by extracting the fundamental frequency at each analysis frame and averaging the values. It persists as a standardized speech parameter because it is defined by a repeatable measurement procedure applied to a recorded speech sample. e.g.: the speaking fundamental frequency measured in a patient during a voice assessment; the speaking fundamental frequency used as a baseline in a voice disorder diagnostic report; the speaking fundamental frequency compared before and after voice therapy | not: jitter (cycle-to-cycle variation of the fundamental frequency, not its mean); pitch (the perceptual attribute of fundamental frequency, not the measured parameter itself) [formal: f0 | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: sound-pressure-level
payload.scope: Sound pressure level is a human-made acoustic parameter — the logarithmic measure of the sound pressure of the voice signal relative to a reference pressure — devised to quantify voice amplitude in acoustic analysis.

definition.body: Sound pressure level is a human-made acoustic parameter of voice: the logarithmic measure of the sound pressure of the voice signal relative to a reference pressure, expressed in decibels. It is computed from a recorded voice signal by measuring the root-mean-square sound pressure of the voice waveform and converting it to a decibel scale using the standard reference pressure of 20 micropascals. It persists as a standardized acoustic parameter because it is defined by a repeatable measurement procedure applied to a recorded voice sample. e.g.: the sound pressure level measured in a patient's voice during a clinical voice assessment; the sound pressure level used as a calibration reference in a voice recording system; the sound pressure level compared across speaking conditions in a voice disorder study | not: intensity (the power per unit area of a sound wave, not its logarithmic measure); loudness (the perceptual attribute of sound pressure level, not the measured parameter itself) [formal: level | substrate: matter | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]
